## 1. Element-Failure Analysis: What the Pack Does and Does Not Establish About the Taking
<a id="element-failure"></a>

The fictional charging sheet alleges that on 12 April 2021 Morgan Ellis took copper fittings belonging to the North Wharf Cooperative, and it states that the sheet does not prove the allegation (`P-FX-CHARGE`, citing `E-FX-CHARGE`). The State bears the burden of proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. That is stated here as the general defense posture; neither fixture rule supplies it, and the elements of the fictional offense, including whether intent to deprive is one, are unverified research items. Fixture rule FX-SUP-1 says only that, for this exercise, a taking count requires proof that the accused carried away property the charge identifies (`P-FX-RULE-SUP`). Fixture rule FX-ADV-1 says that an unexplained departure while carrying a container is enough to submit a taking count (`P-FX-RULE-ADV`). Both are fictional and unverified, and the defense position is tested against each as if it applied.

The State's strongest account comes from Avery Chen, who states that at about 21:10 Chen saw Ellis leave by the north ramp carrying a crate labeled copper fittings, and who also states that Chen did not see what was inside the crate (`P-FX-CHEN`, citing `E-FX-CHEN`). Read with FX-ADV-1, that account describes a departure while carrying a labeled container, and the State may argue it is circumstantial evidence of a taking whose weight is for the fact-finder. The pack contains no explicit statement of Ellis's intention (`P-FX-NO-STATE`), but the absence of such a statement does not remove the adverse circumstantial weight of the labeled crate; the weight is contested and unresolved. What Chen's account does not do is establish what the crate held. A label describes what a container is said to hold and is not a source's observation of its contents.

Samir Patel gives a different account: at about 21:40 Patel saw Ellis leave by the south stair carrying an unmarked canvas bag, did not see a crate, and does not know whether anyone left by the north ramp (`P-FX-PATEL`, citing `E-FX-PATEL`). Camera NW-2 recorded a person in a gray coat at the south stair at 21:41, and the log neither names the person nor describes what the person carried (`P-FX-VIDEO`, citing `E-FX-VIDEO`). The pack does not establish whether Chen and Patel describe the same departure or separate moments (`P-FX-SAME-DEPARTURE`). The State may fairly contend that the observations are compatible, because Patel disclaims knowledge about the north ramp and the log does not identify the person. The defense may fairly respond that the observations differ in time, exit, and container, and that the pack does not resolve which departure the State relies on or what container it alleges (`P-FX-CONTAINER`). Neither side's reading is shown by the sources, and clock calibration between the accounts has not been checked.

The charging sheet names a storeroom inventory as Exhibit S-4 and states that S-4 is not included in the pack (`E-FX-CHARGE`, `P-FX-MISSING`, citing `E-FX-INVENTORY-MISSING`). Its contents, and whether it was collected or disclosed, are unknown. The pack therefore cannot show whether an inventory would confirm or undercut a shortfall, and no conclusion should be drawn about what S-4 would show. If FX-ADV-1 applied, Chen's account might be enough to submit the count without the inventory, and the defense would then rely on credibility, the unresolved event identity, and the limits of what Chen saw. The recommendation is to investigate: obtain S-4 or its status, test the timing and layout, and verify the burden, element, corpus delicti, and admissibility standards before deciding whether and how to move for judgment of acquittal.

## 2. Intent-Gap Analysis: Investigative Omission Versus Misconduct (Test C)
<a id="intent-gap"></a>

The investigating officer, Loren Voss, wrote in a note that Chen told the truth, that Patel is lying to protect Ellis, and that Voss did not ask Patel why the times differ (`P-FX-VOSS`, citing `E-FX-VOSS`). The note's last line states that it does not say Voss wrote Chen's statement or labeled a crate (`E-FX-VOSS-LIMIT`). That line limits what the note says. It is not an exonerating denial and it is not evidence of misconduct, and it is neither proof nor disproof of anything Voss did.

The defense applies evidence-proportionate grading to this record (`P-FX-NO-MISCONDUCT`). The five tiers are a working vocabulary for classifying official conduct and are not the accused's statutory mens rea. The pack contains no evidence that Voss fabricated Chen's statement, tampered with anything, or acted with corrupt intent, so a pretrial motion for sanctions or bad-faith dismissal would have no evidentiary support here, could cost credibility, and could reveal cross-examination themes early. The standard for any such motion is also unverified for the Fixture State.

The supported criticism is narrower: the note records a credibility conclusion about both witnesses and states that Voss did not ask Patel why the times differ. Confirmation bias is a hypothesis for cross-examination about that omission. It is not a finding, and an omission does not prove motive, so Voss's official intent remains unresolved.

The State has a legitimate response, and it is a hypothesis rather than a fact in the sources. The State may argue that a short note may not record the whole inquiry and may reflect an early or partial impression; that Voss may have had grounds for crediting Chen over Patel that this pack does not show; and that if Chen and Patel saw different moments, then Patel's account does not contradict Chen, so not asking about the time difference would be immaterial. The pack establishes none of those grounds, the date of the note, or the completeness of the inquiry. The defense does not claim the pack disproves them. Its answer rests on what the note actually says: Voss recorded that Voss did not ask Patel why the times differ. Other inquiries are unknown. Before arguing that the investigation was incomplete, the defense needs the records of when the note was written, what else was done, and Voss's account of why Patel's statement was discounted. If the observations turn out to be compatible, the omission matters less, which depends on the unresolved question in `P-FX-SAME-DEPARTURE`. The recommendation is to reject any misconduct-sanctions motion on this pack and to preserve the note's recorded omission for cross-examination, subject to verified evidence rules.

## 3. Procedural Remedy: Possible Request for Clarification or a Bill of Particulars
<a id="procedural-remedy"></a>

The charging sheet alleges one taking on 12 April 2021 (`P-FX-CHARGE`), while discovery contains Chen's north-ramp account at about 21:10 with a crate labeled copper fittings (`P-FX-CHEN`) and Patel's south-stair account at about 21:40 with an unmarked canvas bag (`P-FX-PATEL`). The record does not establish whether these describe the same event or separate moments (`P-FX-SAME-DEPARTURE`).

The defense could ask the State which occurrence and which container it relies on. The vehicle for such a request, the showing it requires, its timing, and the court's discretion are all unverified for the Fixture State, and neither fixture rule supplies any of them. The court may deny or defer the request. The trade-offs are real. Moving before trial may disclose the defense's discrepancy theory and give the State time to re-interview witnesses or adjust its proof. Waiting preserves cross-examination but may forgo clarity. The State may also answer that the accounts are compatible, and that answer could weaken the discrepancy theory. Whether a grant would limit evidence of the occurrence the State does not select is also unverified.

A request for the production status of Exhibit S-4 is a separate discovery inquiry and should be kept apart from any request about which occurrence the State relies on. If clarification is denied or deferred, the defense may consider asking for a unanimity instruction. That is a candidate only if the trial evidence actually presents more than one act, verified Fixture State law on duplicity and unanimity supports an instruction and its wording, and the local procedure for requesting and preserving instructions is followed. Any wording should refer only to the acts and containers the trial evidence supports. The recommendation is to investigate: identify the vehicle, deadline, showing, and discretion standard, and decide after that research whether the disclosure cost is worth the possible clarification.
